body_ar: · سؤال: حدود الربح؟. · الجواب: ينظر فيه إلى المادة، فالله سبحانه وتعالى جعلنا خلفاء في الأرض وجعل أصول المنافع التي يحتاج إليها الناس هي ما ضمن الله لآدم في الجنة عندما قال "إن لك أن لا تجوع فهيا ولا تعرى وأنك لا تظمأ فيها ولا تضحى"، فهذه الأربع هي أصول المنافع، فإذا عمل الإنسان ما يحقق منفعة من هذه المنافع له أن يربح بدون حدود، كالذي يزرع فما قطعته من مزرعتك لك الحق أن تبيعه بما شئت أنت، وكذلك الذي يصنع للناس لباسا أو بناء أو ما يحتاجون إليه فله الحق أن يبيعه بما شاء ومثل ذلك الذي يستورد المصنع فيجلبه ويأتي به فهذا يبيع بما شاء وليس للدولة التسعير في حقه وليس للناس ذلك فقد أخرج الترمذي وغيره من حديث أنس بن مالك رضي الله عنه قال غلا السعر على عهد رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم بالمدينة فقلنا يارسول اله سعر لنا فقال "إن الله هو الحي القيوم الخالق الرازق وإنه لأرجو أن ألقى الله غدا وليس أحدا منكم يطالبني بمظلمة في نفس أو مال"، لكن ما جلبته الدولة لها الحق أن تسعره وما صنعته مصانع الدولة لها الحق أن تسعره ومثل ذلك أيضا إذا كان السوق منتظما على سعر معين فجاء من يريد رفع السعر على الناس أو يريد خفضه فللدولة أن تمنع ذلك لما فيه من الفوضى هذا هو المشهور، وقد ذهب ابن رشد الكبير من المالكية إلى أن الرفع ممنوع وأن الخفض مباح، وقد قال محمد عالي ولد عدود رحمة الله عليهما: بحبس ما اشتريته بالبلد *** للربح الاحتكار في البيع احددي وأنت منه مطلقاً في توسعه *** في سعة وامنعه في غير السعه لا فرق في ذلك بين القوت *** وغيره من سائر الوقوت وصانع وزارع من أرضه *** وجالب لقوته وعرضه باعوا أو امسكوا كما قد شاءوا *** وربنا يفعل ما يشاء أما الذي احتيج إلى ذات يده *** باع بسعر وقته في بلده وقل لمن أراد ترخيصاً بع *** كما يبيع الناس أو فارتفع كما رواه مالك عن عمرا *** لذاك قال بعض من تأخرا يمنع ترخيص القليل إن أضر *** بباعة الأسواق رفعاً للضرر وصاحب البيان سام بالغلط *** من لام من سامح في البيع وحط وقال بل مشكور أو مأجور *** وإنما يزجر من يجور.
body_en:
Question: The limits of profit?

Answer: One looks in this to the commodity. God, glorified and exalted, made us successors on the earth, and made the fundamental benefits that people need to be what God guaranteed to Adam in the Garden when He said: {Indeed, it is yours that you shall not go hungry therein, nor go unclothed, and that you shall not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun} (Sūrat Ṭā Hā 20:118–119). These four are the fundamental benefits.

So if a person does work that realises one of these benefits, he may profit without limit. Take one who farms: whatever you have cut from your field, you have the right to sell it for whatever you wish. Likewise one who makes clothing for people, or building, or whatever they need — he has the right to sell it for what he wishes. And so too with one who imports the manufactured article and brings it in and fetches it: this man sells for what he wishes, and the state has no right to fix a price (tasʿīr) in his regard, and neither do the people. For al-Tirmidhi and others narrated, from the hadith of Anas ibn Malik (may God be pleased with him), that he said: prices rose in the time of the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) in Medina, and we said, "Messenger of God, fix prices for us," and he said: "God is the Living, the Self-Subsisting, the Creator, the Provider; and I hope indeed that I shall meet God tomorrow with none of you claiming against me a wrong done in life or in property."

But what the state has itself brought in, it has the right to set a price for; and what the state's own factories have made, it has the right to set a price for. And likewise, if the market is settled at a certain price and someone comes wanting to raise the price on people, or wanting to lower it, the state may prevent that, because of the disorder in it. This is the well-known position (al-mashhūr). Ibn Rushd the Elder, of the Malikis, held that raising the price is barred and that lowering it is permissible (mubāḥ).

Muhammad Ali Ould Addoud (may God's mercy be upon them both) said:

*Define hoarding (iḥtikār) in trade as the withholding of what you have bought in the town, for the sake of profit. Of that you are entirely free in a time of abundance: allow it in plenty and bar it when there is no plenty. In this there is no difference between staple food and anything else among the provisions. A manufacturer, a farmer working his own land, one who brings in his own food and his own goods — they may sell or hold back as they please, and our Lord does what He wills. But as for the man whose stock is needed, he sells at the price of his own time in his own town. And say to whoever means to undercut: sell as the people sell, or else withdraw — as Malik narrated it from ʿUmar. For that reason some of the later scholars said: the small trader is barred from undercutting if it harms the sellers in the markets, so as to lift the harm. And the author of al-Bayān charged with error anyone who blamed a man for being easy in a sale and coming down in his price, and said: rather he is thanked, or rewarded; it is only the man who acts unjustly who is to be restrained.*

flags.arabic: إن لك أن لا تجوع فهيا ولا تعرى وأنك لا تظمأ فيها ولا تضحى
flags.context: the Qur'anic quotation carrying the argument about the four fundamental benefits
options: read فهيا as فيها ('therein'), a transposition of letters
treat فهيا as an unknown word and leave the lacuna visible
flags.note: SOURCE DEFECT (house rule 11): the CMS text has فهيا where Sūrat Ṭā Hā 20:118 has فيها. Preserved unchanged in body_ar; the English translates the Qur'anic text. Also note the source runs 20:118 and 20:119 together as one quotation, which is how the Sheikh cites it.
SOURCE DEFECT (house rule 11): dropped letter in the divine name, an obvious CMS typing error. Preserved in body_ar, translated normally.

flags.arabic: محمد عالي ولد عدود رحمة الله عليهما
options: 'upon them both' refers to Muhammad Ali Ould Addoud and Ibn Rushd the Elder, named in the sentence before
'upon them both' refers to Muhammad Ali Ould Addoud and his father or another figure the Sheikh has in mind
the dual is a slip for the singular عليه
flags.note: The dual pronoun has no certain referent in the text as it stands. Muhammad Ali Ould Addoud (d. 2009) was a senior Mauritanian scholar and a relative of the Sheikh, and this is his versified fiqh. Left as a dual in English ('upon them both') rather than resolved. The Sheikh's office can say who is meant.

flags.context: لا فرق في ذلك بين القوت *** وغيره من سائر الوقوت
options: read as الأقوات, 'the provisions' or 'foodstuffs', which the sense and the rhyme both want
an otherwise unattested plural of وقت, 'times'
flags.note: The line contrasts القوت (the staple) with everything else, so a plural of قوت is required; الوقوت is not a standard plural and may be a transmission error in the CMS or in the Sheikh's quotation from memory. Translated on the required sense and flagged rather than emended.

flags.arabic: يمنع ترخيص القليل إن أضر بباعة الأسواق
flags.context: the later scholars' qualification quoted in the verse
options: the small trader is barred from undercutting if it harms the market sellers
undercutting on a small quantity is barred if it harms the market sellers
a small reduction in price is barred if it harms the market sellers
flags.note: القليل can be the man with little stock, the small quantity, or the small reduction, and the three give materially different rules. The first is taken because the preceding lines are about classes of seller, but the Arabic does not settle it.

flags.context: وصاحب البيان سام بالغلط من لام من سامح في البيع وحط
options: Ibn Rushd the Elder, author of al-Bayān wa-l-Taḥṣīl
another author of a work called al-Bayān
flags.note: 'The author of al-Bayān' is almost certainly Ibn Rushd the Elder, whom the Sheikh has just named, and the position quoted in the verse is consistent with the one he attributes to him. The verse does not name him, so the identification is not made in the English text itself. Note that the verse's ruling and the position the Sheikh attributes to Ibn Rushd in his own prose are close but not identical: the prose says lowering is permissible, the verse says the later scholars bar undercutting where it harms other sellers and that the author of al-Bayān rejected blaming the man who lowers his price.

flags.context: أن الرفع ممنوع وأن الخفض مباح
flags.note: مباح is rendered by its fixed English, 'permissible'. ممنوع is not one of the five rulings and is rendered 'barred' so that the pair is not read as ḥarām/mubāḥ. This is an attributed position, Ibn Rushd's, not the Sheikh's own.

translator_notes: The structure of the answer must survive: unrestricted profit for the producer, the farmer, the maker and the importer; a right of price-fixing for the state only over what it has itself imported or manufactured, and over a settled market against someone moving the price in either direction; then the well-known position (al-mashhūr), then Ibn Rushd's different position, then the versified statement. The position the Sheikh gives as al-mashhūr is the school's, not necessarily his own, and he does not say in this text which he adopts.

The verse (nazm) is rendered as prose in italics per the style guide, with no attempt at English rhyme. The Arabic is preserved line by line in body_ar, with the source's *** hemistich separators intact.
التسعير is the technical term for the authority fixing a price; rendered 'fixing a price' rather than 'price control', which imports a modern regulatory frame the Arabic does not carry.

خلفاء في الأرض rendered 'successors on the earth' rather than 'vicegerents', which overstates what the word does here — the argument only needs that the earth's goods were committed to human management.
Qur'anic renderings are interpretive and are not a substitute for the Arabic.
